$comment: The upstream revisions this repository's ports are built against, in machine-readable form.
Every one of these checkouts is gitignored (see `.gitignore`: `.ref/`), so a CI runner starts
with none of them and must fetch the exact commit recorded here. That makes this file the
single place where 'which upstream' is answered, and it is what the scheduled drift check
(.github/workflows/check-upstream-drift.yml) diffs against the live remotes: if a branch has
moved past the commit below, an engine is out of date and only that engine needs rebuilding.
`engine` names the build workflow to dispatch for that checkout, and the key under `engines`
is the engine name used by ports/lib/fetch-engine.mjs. `full-clone` marks checkouts that
cannot be fetched shallowly: a shallow clone of vcpkg makes its own `read-tree` fail with
exit code 128 while resolving its baseline, so it must be a full clone.
EVERY KEY UNDER `engines` IS DISPATCHABLE, AND THAT IS WHY ARTEMIS IS NOT ONE OF THEM
check-drift.mjs does not consult `publish-gated` or any other flag: it iterates every key of
`engines` (line 114, `Object.entries(pins.engines)`), requires repository/branch/commit, and for
any engine whose pinned commit is no longer the branch head it pushes that engine's `workflow`
into the matrix the drift job fans out over -- which then runs `gh workflow run <that path>`.
So an `engines` entry is a promise that a workflow by that name exists, and it must be deleted
in the same commit that deletes the workflow.
The artemis-compat host build (a browser host patched onto the third-party sources, artifact
`artemis-web-android.wasm`) is retired, and with it `.github/workflows/build-wasm-artemis.yml`
and `.github/scripts/build-artemis.sh`. Leaving the entry behind would have made the daily
cron dispatch a workflow that no longer exists the next time artemis-compat moved.
BOTH Artemis records below are SIBLINGS of `engines`, never iterated by the drift check, and
that is deliberate rather than an oversight: each one builds a patch or patch-set of the same
upstream, and an upstream move does not make that patch apply. Dispatching them on drift would
pair an unreviewed engine revision with reviewed patches, which is the one combination neither
record describes. Moving either pin is a hand edit that rebases the patches and reruns the
gates.
`artemis-compat` is the SHIPPING record: the browser worker built by compiling the upstream
engine source itself (plus the patch set and overlays in `ports/artemis/compat-web/`) rather
than the official proprietary SDK module. It is named `artemis-compat`, not added under
`engines`, precisely so that adding a shipping build does not create a new entry in the
engine-name enum or an automatic dispatch contract. The artifact is NOT an engine-SDK build,
and it is also not published yet: `publish: false` stays until a real game boots on it.
`artemis-bridge` is the LEGACY record: it recompiles the retained official asyncify module on
top of the hand-written engine in `ports/artemis/src`, which is a different (and unresolved)
redistribution question. It is manual / diagnostic only -- `build-wasm-artemis-bridge.yml` no
longer runs on push or pull_request -- and it is NOT the shipping statement of how this
repository obtains Artemis. Nothing downstream may read it as one.
Do not edit `commit` by hand to silence the drift check. Moving a pin means rebuilding the
engine, re-running its gates, and publishing a new manifest -- the commit recorded here is
the one the published bytes were built from.

vcpkg.why: kirikiroid2-web/vcpkg-configuration.json pins this commit as its builtin-registry baseline, and a shallow clone cannot resolve it.

wabt.why: wasm2c regenerates the Artemis bridge's C source from the vendored SDK modules.

$comment: The shipping Artemis record. Unlike `artemis-bridge` this is a source build: the tracked
input is the upstream engine at the commit below plus `ports/artemis/compat-web/`, and the
produced module is what a browser host is meant to run.
`workflow` names the workflow that owns this build; `dispatch: false` is the drift contract
spelled out, because this is a sibling of `engines` and the drift check never sees it. The
two are still checked against the filesystem by scripts/check-sources.mjs, so a record
pointing at a workflow that was deleted fails the source gate.
`git-archive` records what the workflow's `skip-upstream-checkout: true` assumes: the
compat-web recipe clones the pin itself, shallowly, and archives it by hash. It has to stay
`true` -- with the reusable workflow's own checkout the recipe would receive the engine at
the pin but with compat-web's overlays missing, i.e. a different build input than the one
the artifact hash describes.
There is deliberately no `module` / `expected` hash block here. The old Artemis entry
carried md5s of a 103 MB transpile; this build has no transpile, and its output hashes are
produced per run and published in the artifact's own manifest.
The bridge is not an engine build: it recompiles the official Artemis module from its
wasm2c-transpiled form on top of the hand-written engine in ports/artemis/src. Its only
input that is not tracked is the 103 MB transpile, and that is regenerable byte-for-byte,
so the workflow produces it instead of downloading it.
The upstream pin is recorded beside this entry as `artemis-compat`, and it is the SAME
commit: the pin describes the artemis-compat checkout both builds take their inputs from.
The copy here is what this workflow passes. The bridge is legacy/diagnostic only, is not
the shipping Artemis path, and no longer runs on push or pull_request -- see the workflow.
The md5 values are the reference transpiles' hashes, measured on this machine against
wabt at the commit above. They are recorded so the workflow can assert it regenerated the
same bytes rather than a merely-similar file: wasm2c derives the emitted
`#include "artemis.wasm2c.h"` from the `-o` basename, so any other output name yields a
file that differs by about 30 bytes and does not compile.
